html:
An ancient city on the inland delta of the Niger River in Mali, settled around 250 BCE and abandoned around 1400. It is one of the oldest known cities in Africa south of the Sahara.

Excavations by the archaeologists Susan and Roderick McIntosh from the late 1970s changed ideas about West Africa. Older theories held that towns there grew up only after Arab traders arrived across the Sahara. Djenné-Djenno was already a busy town centuries before that. At its height, around 800 CE, thousands of people lived there and in clusters of villages around it.

Its people grew African rice, fished, herded and worked iron. They traded for copper, stone and salt from far away, and glass beads from even further. Yet the town had no palace, citadel or great temple. It seems to have been a city of many specialised groups without a ruling class.

The site was abandoned as the new town of Djenné grew nearby. Djenné, with its Great Mosque, became a trading partner of Timbuktu in the age of the Mali Empire. Looters have since damaged the old site.
sum: An ancient city on the inland delta of the Niger River in Mali, settled around 250 BCE and abandoned around 1400. It is one of the oldest known cities in Africa south of the Sahara.
